The nitrate ion has three resonance structures. In each one there is **one N=O** double bond
and **two N–O** single bonds, and the double bond moves round the three oxygens in turn.

negative charge and the extra bond are **delocalised** evenly over the three N–O links.

= (1 double + 2 single) ÷ 3
= 4 ÷ 3
= **1·33** ✓

really were double, that one would be measurably shorter, and it is not.

nitrogen overlaps sideways with all three oxygens at once to give the delocalised π system.

is the value for a species averaging over **two** links, such as the nitrite ion NO₂⁻.
∴ 1·33.

The boiling points of the hydrogen halides are
**HF 19·5 °C**, HCl −85 °C, HBr −67 °C, HI −35 °C
Room temperature is about 25 °C, so only **HF**, boiling at 19·5 °C, is anywhere near being a
liquid — and below 19·5 °C it is one ✓ The other three are gases at room temperature by a
margin of sixty degrees or more.
The reason HF stands so far out of line is **hydrogen bonding**. Fluorine is the most
electronegative element, so the H–F bond is strongly polarised and the small, bare proton can
approach the lone pair of a fluorine on the next molecule closely. HF molecules therefore
associate into zig-zag chains (HF)ₙ, and boiling means breaking those hydrogen bonds as well
as the ordinary van der Waals forces.
Chlorine, bromine and iodine are too large and too weakly electronegative for this, so HCl,
HBr and HI are held only by dipole-dipole and dispersion forces.
The same anomaly makes HF a **weak** acid in water while the other three are strong, and it
is why water and ammonia boil far above the hydrides below them in their groups.
∴ HF.

weakest intermolecular forces and boils lowest.

The bond dissociation enthalpies are
F–F **155** kJ mol⁻¹
Br–Cl **218** kJ mol⁻¹
Br–F **237** kJ mol⁻¹
**Cl–F 253 kJ mol⁻¹** ✓ the strongest

interhalogen compound.
Two things are going on.
**F–F is anomalously weak.** You would expect the bond between the two smallest atoms to be
the strongest, and it is the weakest of all. Fluorine is so small that the three lone pairs
on each atom are forced close together, and their mutual repulsion across the short bond
largely cancels the bonding. The same weakness makes F₂ extraordinarily reactive.
**Interhalogen bonds are stronger than either parent.** The two atoms differ in
electronegativity, so the bond has partial ionic character, which adds to its strength. The
larger the difference, the greater that contribution — but it works against the fact that a
longer bond is a weaker one.
Between Cl–F and Br–F the two effects pull opposite ways: Br–F has the larger electronegativity
difference, but Cl–F is the **shorter** bond, and the shortness wins.
∴ Cl–F.

Percent ionic character compares the **measured** dipole moment with the one the molecule
would have if the bond were **completely ionic** — that is, if a whole electronic charge sat
on each atom.
**Step 1 — the dipole moment of a fully ionic Li⁺H⁻.**
μ(ionic) = e × d
with e = 1·602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and d = 1·6 Å = 1·6 × 10⁻¹⁰ m
μ(ionic) = 1·602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1·6 × 10⁻¹⁰
= 2·56 × 10⁻²⁹ C m
**Step 2 — compare with the observed value.**
% ionic character = (μ observed / μ ionic) × 100
= (2·0 × 10⁻²⁹ / 2·56 × 10⁻²⁹) × 100
= 0·78 × 100
= **78 % ≈ 80 %** ✓
The one step that is easy to get wrong is the ångström: 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m, so 1·6 Å is
1·6 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, not 1·6 × 10⁻⁹.
A bond 78 % ionic is very ionic indeed, which fits: lithium is the least electronegative
element in the second period and LiH is a salt-like hydride that reacts violently with water
to give H₂.
∴ 80 %.

A molecule is **non-polar** when its bond moments cancel, which needs a **symmetrical** shape —
and the shape is decided by the lone pairs on the central atom.
**I. NCl₃** — nitrogen has 5 valence electrons, 3 used in bonds, leaving **1 lone pair**.
3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair ⇒ **pyramidal**. The lone pair breaks the symmetry, so the bond
moments cannot cancel: NCl₃ is **polar**, μ ≈ 0·6 D ✗
**II. SO₃** — sulphur has 6 valence electrons, all 6 committed to three S=O bonds, so **no
lone pair**. 3 bond pairs ⇒ **trigonal planar**, three identical moments at 120° cancelling
exactly: **non-polar**, μ = 0 ✓
**III. PCl₅** — phosphorus has 5 valence electrons, all 5 bonded, **no lone pair**.
5 bond pairs ⇒ **trigonal bipyramidal**. The three equatorial moments at 120° cancel among
themselves, and the two axial moments are exactly opposite and cancel each other:
**non-polar**, μ = 0 ✓
So the non-polar ones are **II and III**.
The contrast between NCl₃ and the other two is the lesson: NH₃ and NCl₃ are pyramidal and
polar, while SO₃ and PCl₅ have no lone pair and are symmetrical.
∴ II and III only.

Note: the printed key gives (c), I and II. NCl₃ is pyramidal because of its lone pair and has
a measurable dipole moment, so it is polar; the key is wrong and has been corrected to (d).
